# The appointments Máni made — and who is keeping them

One myth is a story. A cycle of myths is a specification. Read Máni's cycle in order and the industries fall out of it one by one.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Máni
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Domain of influence:** Moon, Night, Time
- **Pattern seats:** 3
- **Sectors touched:** Technology & Innovation · Culture & Entertainment · Health & Wellbeing
- **Strongest seat:** Space, Astronomy & Celestial Science
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 218 of 397

## The Cycle, Read Forward

### Space, Astronomy & Celestial Science — through *Mundilfari's Boast*

In the Vafþrúðnismál, the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike.  Snorri, in Gylfaginning, gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The moon personified, driving its chariot across the night sky — the Norse moon made god, pursued nightly by Hati.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. Industries do not invent their archetypes; they inherit them and call them best practice.

### Timekeeping & Calendar Systems — through *The Wolf at the Moon's Heels*

The moon does not drift; it flees.  Snorri explains its speed by its hunter: two wolves run with the lights of heaven, and Hati Hróðvitnisson is the one who runs before the moon and means to take it — 'and so it will come to pass.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *Moon and month share his name's root in every Germanic language; the first calendar counted by his phases.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. The trade thinks it is optimizing a process. It is re-enacting a charter.

### Sleep & Recovery Technology — through *Bil and Hjúki at the Well*

Snorri records that Máni took two children up from the earth, Bil and Hjúki, as they walked from the well called Byrgir, carrying on their shoulders the pail Sægr — often read as a mead-tub — slung from the pole Simul.  Their father is named Viðfinnr.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The night watch himself; the moon that governs every sleeping hour is his face.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. That is the cycle working: story becomes duty, duty becomes trade.

## The Theme That Runs the Cycle

Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him three scenes — a father's fatal boast, a wolf's patient pursuit, and two children lifted from a well — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face. Around those scenes gathers the quieter charge the Vafþrúðnismál records: the gods shaped the new and waning moons so that men could reckon their years.

## The Method, Stated Plainly

The atlas is not a horoscope. Seats are earned from the sources — argued, weighted, published — and every one of them can be challenged at the [methodology page](/patterns/methodology/). A match that cannot survive an argument does not survive review. That is the whole trick: the patterns are claims, and claims can be tested.

## For the Ones Who Work There

If you work in space, astronomy & celestial science, timekeeping & calendar systems, or any trade this temple holds a seat in, this is the honest version of what a placement means: your industry beside the story it has been re-telling all along — on the temple floor itself, before an audience that came specifically to read it. The [patron tier](/sites/mani/patron/) and the [advertising terms](/terms/advertising/) describe the mechanics; the resonance above describes the fit.
